title-group.article-title: Optimization of Active Distribution Network Operation with SOP Considering Reverse Power Flow

abstract.p: As the penetration of distributed renewable energy increases, the phenomenon of bidirectional power flow in distribution networks becomes increasingly severe. Traditional regulation devices like OLTC (on-load tap changer) and CB (capacitor bank) cannot effectively mitigate reverse power flow in distribution networks due to their limitations. The transmission capacity of the distribution network under reverse power flow is approximately 50% of the rated capacity of the OLTC, leading to issues such as voltage limit violations and high wind and solar curtailment rates. This paper proposes a method for calculating the reverse power flow delivery capacity of distribution networks, quantitatively describing the distribution network’s delivery limits for reverse power flow. Based on this, a joint optimization model for multiple distribution networks with an SOP is established. The SOP is utilized to share reverse power flow delivery capacity among multiple distribution networks, enhancing operational economy and increasing the accommodation of the DG. Finally, the method’s effectiveness and correctness are verified in the IEEE 33-node system. The results validate that while joint operation does not enhance the reverse flow transmission capacity of a single distribution network, it can, through the shared reverse flow transmission capacity approach, elevate the reverse flow transmission capacity to approximately 70% during the majority of time periods.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: In recent years, as environmental issues such as global warming become increasingly severe, the distributed generation (DG) of distributed renewable energy sources has rapidly developed [1,2,3]. The distribution network, as the main carrier of the DG, has seen a continuous increase in the penetration rate of the DG within it [4]. This has highlighted the issue of bidirectional power flow [5] in distribution networks, which can, in severe cases, lead to over-voltage problems [6]. When confronted with significant reverse power flows, traditional regulatory equipment like on-load tap changer (OLTC) and capacitor bank (CB) exhibit slow regulation speeds, an inability to output continuously, and limited operational ranges [7,8,9,10,11,12]. Consequently, the distribution network’s capacity to handle reverse power flow is insufficient, leading to voltage limit violations, wind and solar curtailments, and other issues that hinder the further development of the distribution network.

In addressing the aforementioned challenges, flexible distribution devices, exemplified by soft open point (SOP) [13], have garnered significant attention in recent years. SOPs, composed of fully controllable power electronic devices, are free from the operation frequency limitations of traditional mechanical switches. They allow rapid and precise control [14,15] of active and reactive power on connected feeders, making them an excellent choice for addressing supply–demand imbalances in distribution networks, thereby greatly enhancing network operational efficiency [16,17,18]. Considerable research has already been conducted on SOP in distribution network optimization. For instance, the literature [19,20] explores the working principle of SOPs in network optimization and establishes an optimal scheduling model by coordinating various controllable resources, thus achieving optimal power flow distribution. The literature [21] proposes a time-segmented reactive compensation strategy. By joint optimization of an SOP and energy storage systems, targeting minimization of average voltage deviation and network loss, operational efficiency is enhanced. The literature [22] develops a two-stage day-ahead and intra-day optimization model incorporating an SOP and other flexible resources, with distributed generation (DG) penetration as the objective function, improving economic efficiency while boosting DG accommodation. The literature [23] establishes an active–reactive coordination optimization model for the network, resolving voltage limit issues by regulating reactive compensation devices, photovoltaic inverters, SOPs, and other adjustable equipment. Additionally, several studies, including [24], address voltage issues arising from two-way power flow due to increased DG penetration by establishing a bidirectional transformer model to quantify control curves under bidirectional flow and mitigating voltage fluctuations through multi-layer regulation of energy storage devices. However, there is limited research on detailed modeling of reverse power flow transmission capacity in distribution networks and on utilizing SOP flexibility to address challenges of insufficient reverse power flow transmission capability.

Based on the aforementioned issues, this paper’s contributions are as follows:(1)
It analyzes the impact of OLTC parameters, the OLTC’s low-voltage side reactive compensation, and DG installation location on the reverse power flow capacity of distribution networks. A refined model is established, enabling precise calculations of reverse power flow capacity considering these influencing factors.(2)
Addressing the issue of insufficient reverse power flow capacity in distribution networks, a multi-distribution network joint operation optimization model is established based on an SOP. This interconnects multiple distribution networks via an SOP, enhancing the reverse power flow capacity of individual networks, thus improving the overall operational efficiency of the distribution network.(3)
Using the improved IEEE 33-node system, the paper examines the optimization role of an SOP when introduced in various operational scenarios, impacting the reverse power flow capacity and overall operational efficiency of the distribution network.

sec.title: 2. Analysis of Factors Affecting Reverse Power Flow Transmission Capacity in Distribution Networks
sec.p: Reverse power flow in a distribution network occurs when the output from the DG exceeds the load demand of the distribution network, causing power to flow backward to the upstream grid. The reverse power flow capacity in distribution networks is influenced by the following three factors: The first factor is the parameters of the OLTC connected between the distribution network and the upstream grid, including the rated capacity of the OLTC, the difference in the per unit values of voltage on both sides of the OLTC, as well as the allowable maximum and minimum tap changer ratios. The second factor is the capacity of reactive power compensation that can be deployed on the low-voltage side of the OLTC. The third factor is the electrical distance from the DG to the low-voltage side of the OLTC.

First, the nameplate-rated capacity of the OLTC directly determines the maximum reverse power flow that can be transmitted. Additionally, the magnitude of reverse power flow during transmission is proportional to the difference in the per unit values of voltage on both sides of the OLTC. Therefore, the greater the difference, the larger the reverse power flow capacity. Since the per unit value of the high-voltage side remains constant and is lower than that of the low-voltage side during operation, with increasing transmission capacity, the per unit value of the low-voltage side voltage increases. Consequently, the OLTC’s transformation ratio also increases. When this ratio reaches its upper limit, further increase in reverse power flow capacity is not possible.

Regarding the reactive power compensation capacity on the low-voltage side of the OLTC, to maintain the power factor of the OLTC primary side (low-voltage side during reverse flow) at the required value, as the reverse power flow capacity increases, more reactive compensation capacity is required on the low-voltage side. Once the full compensation capacity is utilized, further increase in reverse power flow capacity is not possible.

Concerning the electrical distance from the DG to the OLTC’s low-voltage side, as the reverse power flow capacity increases, the voltage drop along the line from the DG to OLTC also increases [25]. When this voltage drop reaches its allowable maximum, further increase in transmission capacity necessarily requires reduced allowable electrical distance between the DG and the OLTC to prevent voltage limit violations [26,27]. When the electrical distance is reduced to zero, meaning the DG node coincides with the OLTC’s low-voltage side node, any further capacity increase is not possible.

The circuit diagram in Figure 1 shows the equivalent representation of all distributed generation (DG) and loads in the distribution network. Here, RT*+jXT* denotes the internal impedance of the OLTC, ZDG* refers to the per unit value of the impedance from the equivalent DG source to the OLTC’s low-voltage side, and ZL* represents the impedance from the equivalent DG source to the equivalent load. QC1* and QC2* are the reactive power compensation on the high-voltage and low-voltage sides of the OLTC, respectively. U1*, U2*, and U3* denote the voltage values at the OLTC’s high-voltage side, low-voltage side, and equivalent DG nodes, respectively. S1* and S2* are the magnitudes of the power flow injected into and flowing out of the OLTC under forward power flow conditions. S2,re* and S1,re* represent the apparent power injected into and flowing out of the OLTC during reverse power flow conditions. K* signifies the transformer turns ratio.

sec.p: The OLTC’s rated capacity determines its transmission capacity limit during power flow, regardless of the flow direction. Their values are less than the rated per unit capacity of the OLTC, i.e., less than 1. U1,t* and U2,t* are the peer unit values of the high- and low-voltage sides of the OLTC during period t. dUt* and dUre,t* are the differences in the per unit values of voltages on the high and low sides for forward and reverse flows, respectively. ZT* is the per unit internal impedance of the OLTC. The power factor cosφT is required on the primary side of the OLTC, while cosφZT is the power factor angle of the OLTC internal impedance. It can be observed that regardless of the flow direction, the flow capacity of the OLTC increases as the difference in the per unit voltage values between the high- and low-voltage sides increases.

sec.title: 2.2. Reactive Power Compensation on the Low-Voltage Side of Oil-Immersed Tap Changers Influences Reverse Power Flow Capacity
sec.p: During OLTC operation, reactive power compensation must be applied on both sides to maintain power factor. In the presence of forward power flow, the power factor of the upstream grid might not meet the OLTC’s primary requirements. Hence, reactive power is added on the high-voltage (primary) side to adjust the power factor. Also, considering the mismatch between the OLTC’s low-voltage (secondary) side power factor and the distribution network’s power factor, reactive compensation is introduced on the low-voltage side as well. In reverse power flow scenarios, due to the high-power factor derived from DG units, capacitive reactive power is introduced on the low-voltage (primary) side to lower the power factor. Similarly, as the OLTC’s internal reactive losses surpass active losses, capacitive reactive power is added to the high-voltage (secondary) side to maintain the power factor. To facilitate the analysis of changes in active and reactive power, based on Figure 1, this paper employs the tangent value of the power factor angle to describe the aforementioned compensation process. For forward power flow, the tangent values of the power factor angle on both sides of the OLTC can be expressed as follows:(9)tanφ1,t=Q1,t* P1,t* (10)tanφT=Q1,t* −QC1,t* P1,t* (11)tanφ2,t=Q1,t* −QL1,t* −∆QT,t* +QC2,t* P1,t−∆PT,t (12)∆PT,t* +j∆QT,t* =(P1,t*)2(1+tan2φT)(U1,t*)2·RT* +jXT*

In forward power flow conditions, P1,t* and Q1,t* are the per unit values of active and reactive power injected from the higher-level grid into the high-voltage side. φ1,t represents the power factor angle, φT is the required power factor angle on the primary side of the OLTC, and φ2,t is the required power factor angle on the low-voltage side of the OLTC. QC1,t* and QC2,t* are the per unit values for reactive compensation capacity on the high- and low-voltage sides. ∆PT,t* and ∆QT,t* denote the per unit active and reactive power losses on the OLTC at this time.

Below reverse flow conditions, the tangent of the power factor angle for each node is represented as:(13) tanφ2,re,t=Q2,re,t* P2,re,t* (14)tanφT=Q2,re,t* +QC2,re,t* P2,re,t* (15)tanφ1,re,t=Q2,re,t* +QC2,re,t* −∆QT,re,t* +QC1,re,t* P2,re,t* −∆PT,re,t* (16)∆PT,re,t* +j∆QT,re,t* =P2,re,t* 2(1+tan2φT)(U2,t*)2RT* +jXT*

P2,re,t* and Q2,re,t* represent the per unit active and reactive power injected into the distribution network under reverse power flow at the low-voltage side of the OLTC. φ2,re denotes the power factor angle at this moment, while φ1,re,t indicates the required power factor angle at the high-voltage side at this time. QC1,re,t* and QC2,re,t* represent the per unit reactive compensation capacity at the high- and low-voltage sides at this time. ∆PT,re,t* and ∆QT,re,t* represent the active and reactive power losses on the OLTC at this moment.

The relationship between the per unit values of power flow transfer capacity and reactive power compensation at both ends in positive and negative sequences is derived after arranging Equation (9) through (16) according to the aforementioned relationships. (17)S1,t*=min⁡QL1,t* (tanφ1,t−tanφT)cosφ1,t,QC2,t*−tanφ2RT*+XT* ·1+tan2φT·cos2φ1,t

The OLTC reverse power flow limits, S1,t* and S2,re,t*, represent forward and backward power flow scenarios. Both values increase as the reactive power compensation on the high and low sides increases. When the forward power flow S1,t* reaches the OLTC’s rated capacity (equal to 1), QL1,t* and QC2,t* denote the initial installation capacity on high and low sides. If the reactive power compensation needed for reverse flow exceeds this, the reverse power limit peaks. Equation (18) seeks the maximum S2,re,t* , and hence uses K max*. The real distribution network data of tanφ1,t, tanφT, tanφ2,t, tanφ1,re,t, and tanφ2,re,t show the relationship between power flow limits and reactive compensation, as depicted in Figure 3.

In the diagram, the vertical axis represents the forward and reverse power flow capacities of the OLTC, while the horizontal axis indicates reactive compensation capacities on both sides of the OLTC, with the red and blue curves representing high-voltage and low-voltage sides, respectively. When S1,t* equals 1, the x-coordinate values of the red and blue curves denote the initial reactive compensation installed capacities on the high- and low-voltage sides of the OLTC. Under these installed capacities, the maximum reverse power flow capacity that the low-voltage side can compensate is about 33% of the OLTC’s rated capacity, whereas the high-voltage side can compensate up to approximately 95%. This indicates that the reverse power flow capacity is primarily constrained by the reactive compensation capacity on the low-voltage side of the OLTC. Therefore, Equation (18) can be expressed as:(19) S2,re,t* =QC2,re,t* (tanφT−tanφ2,re,t)cosφ2,re

To enhance the reverse power flow capacity, increase the reactive power compensation installation capacity on the low-voltage side. After increasing the installation capacity, the relationship between S2,re,Q,t* and QC2,re,t* can be seen in Figure 4.

The graph’s horizontal axis represents the reactive power compensation capacity on the OLTC’s low-voltage side, while the vertical axis indicates the reverse power flow transfer capacity. One can observe that S2,re,t* increases with the rise in QC2,re,t*. The horizontal lines from bottom to top signify the maximum S2,re,t* achievable with increasing bt, reflecting the constraint imposed by Kt* in Section 2.1. At this juncture, further escalation of QC2,re,t* does not enhance S2,re,t*. When bt attains its peak value of 1.05, the corresponding QC2,re,t* denotes the maximum installable reactive power compensation capacity on the low-voltage side. At this point, both bt and Kt* reach their limits, and S2,re,t* approaches the OLTC’s boundary, rendering additional reactive compensation futile.

sec.title: 2.3. The Influence of Electrical Distance from DG to Low-Voltage Side of OLTC on Reverse Power Flow Delivery Capacity
sec.p: The electrical distance from the DG to the low-voltage side of the OLTC refers to the impedance relationship between these two points. A greater electrical distance ZDG* implies a larger voltage difference between these points when transmitting power flow, thus reducing the capacity for reverse power flow. The relationship between reverse power flow transmission capacity and the electrical distance from the DG to the low-voltage side of the OLTC can be derived as follows. U3,t*−U2,t*=P2,re,t*RDG*+Q2,re,t*XDG*U2,t*

The differential dU 32,t* refers to the deviation between the voltage of the DG node and the per unit voltage at the low-voltage side of the OLTC. Parameters RDG* and XDG* denote the resistance and reactance from the DG to the OLTC’s low-voltage side, respectively. The power factor of the impedance cosφZDG correlates to the DG towards the OLTC’s low-voltage side impedance. The coefficient cDG is constant, while U3,t* represents the per unit equivalent of the DG node voltage. The aim is to ascertain the maximum achievable S2,re,t* under the influence of ZDG*, leading K t* and U3,t* to be maximized. The maximum U3,t* is detailed in Equation (21). Substituting Equation (21) into Equation (20) yields the relationship between S2,re,t* and ZDG*, as expressed in the equation. It shows an inverse relationship, illustrated in Figure 5, between S2,re,t* and ZDG*.

The horizontal axis represents ZDG*, while the vertical axis denotes S2,re,t*. In the plot, a series of inverse proportional curves showcase the variation of S2,re,t* with ZDG* as bt decreases. As ZDG* increases, S2,re,t* diminishes. Moreover, at a constant ZDG*, larger bt values result in smaller S2,re,t* . This occurs because the maximum ZDG* remains constant, hence as bt increases, the dU 32,t* decreases, thereby reducing S2,re,t* .

sec.title: 3. Actual Maximum Transfer Capacity of Reverse Power Flow in the Distribution Network
sec.p: Section 2.1, Section 2.2 and Section 2.3 analyzed the impacts of the OLTC transformation ratio Kt *, the reactive power compensation capacity on the low-voltage side of the OLTC QC2,re,t* , the electrical distance from the DG to the low-voltage side of the OLTC ZDG*, and the OLTC’s low-voltage side voltage parameter bt on S2,re,t* . Section 2.1 states that S2,re,t* increases with larger Kt * and bt, reaching up to approximately 84% of the OLTC’s rated capacity when both are at maximum values. Section 2.2 explains that increasing Kt * and bt to enhance S2,re,t* requires reactive support from QC2,re,t* on the low-voltage side, necessitating additional reactive equipment, which raises cost. However, given sufficient reactive power, S2,re,t* achieves the maximum value from Section 2.1. Section 2.3 notes that S2,re,t* decreases as ZDG* rises and points out a contradiction with prior conclusions when ZDG* is fixed and a smaller bt results in a larger S2,re,t* .

In the above scenario, analyzing from the perspective of the OLTC, an increase in bt results in a larger S2,re,t* . However, when analyzed from the perspective of the line to the low-voltage side of the DG to OLTC, an increase in bt results in a smaller S2,re,t* . Therefore, it is necessary to select an appropriate bt to maximize S2,re,t* after comprehensively considering various influencing factors. The actual maximum reverse power transfer capacity of distribution networks, S2,re,t,max* , can be expressed as:(23) S2,re,t,max*=min⁡{7,9,(22)} (24)7=9=(22)

Equation (23) elucidates that the value of S2,re,t,max* is determined as the minimum under three distinct constraints. Equation (24) indicates that S2,re,t* should remain equal across the same time period under three different constraints, as they represent the same power flow. Figure 6 demonstrates the relationship among S2,re,t*, QC2,re,t* , ZDG*, and bt when Kt * is set to Kmax *.

The horizontal axis of the graph has its positive direction labeled as ZDG*, and its negative direction is labeled as QC2,re,t* . The vertical axis is S2,re,t*. On the right side of the vertical axis, inverse proportion curves in different colors represent the variation of S2,re,t* with ZDG* under various bt conditions. On the left side, a black linear function indicates the relationship of S2,re,t* with QC2,re,t* under different bt conditions. The colored horizontal lines on both sides of the vertical axis signify the value of S2,re,t* when Kt *=Kmax *, across different bt scenarios. When Kt *=Kmax * and reactive power compensation QC2,re,t* is sufficient, without considering ZDG* constraints, S2,re,t,max* can reach approximately 84% of the OLTC’s rated capacity. However, in practical operation, with ZDG* limitations considered, S2,re,t,max* is limited to about 50% of the OLTC’s rated capacity. Refer to Figure 1 for an equivalent circuit diagram, taking the high-voltage side node of the OLTC as the balance node. The specific calculation process of S2,re,t,max* is illustrated in Table 1.

The specific flowchart is shown in Figure 7. The aforementioned steps calculate the maximum reverse power flow transfer capacity for this distribution network. When the required reverse power flow exceeds this value, the DG output needs reduction. Conversely, if the reverse power flow is less than this value, it can be transferred smoothly. Additionally, the input Kt* in Step 2 can be reduced to optimize the operational cost of the distribution network.

sec.title: 4. Joint Operation Optimization Model for Multi-Distribution Networks with SOP Considering Reverse Power Flow
sec.p: Since the maximum value of S2,re,t,max* in the distribution network is only about 50% of the OLTC’s rated capacity, it limits further development. To address this issue, this paper employs a soft open point (SOP) to flexibly interconnect multiple distribution grids. This enables sharing of backward power transfer capacities among sub-distribution networks and enhances the grid’s capacity to handle reverse flow under high penetration of the DG. Figure 8 illustrates the SOP interconnection schematic, where the SOP interlinks two distribution networks at an equivalent power source node. When the reverse power flow in distribution network 1 exceeds its maximum transferable capacity, the SOP diverts the excess power to distribution network 2, which then transmits it to the upstream grid, thus reducing occurrences of wind and solar energy curtailment.

sec.title: 4.1. Fundamental Principles and Mathematical Models of SOP
sec.p: This paper employs a back-to-back voltage source converter (B2B VSC) to implement the SOP. The number of ports is determined by the count of AC/DC bidirectional converters, which are internally connected through a DC/DC converter. The AC side of the AC/DC converter links to the distribution network feeders, while the DC side connects to the DC/DC converter, enabling interconnection between different feeders. The basic topology is illustrated in the Figure 9.

Under normal operating conditions, the two-end SOP selects a PQ-Vdc control mode, while the three-end SOP employs a PQ-PQ-Vdc Q control mode. This means that one VSC regulates the DC-side voltage, and the other VSCs control the power being transmitted. The operational variables of the SOP include the active and reactive power transmitted by the VSCs, with specific operational constraints as follows [28,29]:(25)∑i∈ΩSOP Pi,tAC−Pi,t,lossAC=0 (26)SiAC≥Pi,tAC2+Qi,tAC2 (27)SiAC≥Pi,tAC≥−SiAC (28)SiAC≥Qi,tAC≥−SiAC

The set ΩSOP contains the port nodes of the SOP. The terms Pi,tAC and Qi,tAC represent the active and reactive power injected by port i of the SOP at time period t. The terms PtDC and Pt,lossSOP are the active power injected by the SOP’s DC/DC converter and the total active power loss at time period t, respectively. The variable SiAC denotes the capacity of the AC/DC converter at port i of the SOP, and SDC represents the capacity of the SOP’s DC/DC converter. When the SOP transmits a significant amount of power, its internal power loss becomes non-negligible. Given that multiple VSCs are identical in model and symmetrically positioned, the analysis focuses on one VSCi, and its equivalent model is illustrated in Figure 10.

In the Figure 10, Si1 represents the SOP bus’s injected SOP power, while Si2 denotes the apparent power injected by the VSC at the converter bus. Ui1∠δ1 and Ui2∠δ2 correspond to the voltage and phase angle at the SOP bus and VSC bus, respectively. The phase angle difference Δδ indicates the phase angle of VSC pulse modulation, determining the magnitude and direction of SOP injected power. Udc and Idc stand for the DC-side current and voltage of the VSC, and gDC represents the equivalent conductance on the VSC’s DC side. RVSC and XVSC are the equivalent resistance and reactance of the VSC. Specific constraints include:

sec.p: The active power loss of VSC equates to the power injected on the AC side minus the power injected on the DC side. In the context of SOP involvement in distribution network optimization, there are five unknowns in the five constraints stated above. When employing PQ control, the unknowns are: Udc, Idc, Ploss,i, Δδ, and Mi. Under QU control, the unknowns are: Pi1, Idc, Ploss,i, Δδ, and Mi, which can be solved based on optimization results.

sec.title: 4.2. Objective Function
sec.p: The objective function aims to minimize the sum of the daily comprehensive operating costs of multiple distribution networks after joint operation. The daily comprehensive operating costs include: network loss cost μlossPm,tloss, wind and solar curtailment cost μDGPDG,m,tloss, and device (SOP, CB, OLTC) operation cost COP,m,t, as expressed in the following equation:(34)minFm=∑m=1Ω∑t=1T(μlossPm,t*loss+μDGPDG,m,t*loss+COP,m,t) (35)Pm,t*loss=∑ij=ΩBIm,ij,t*2rm,ij* (36)Pm,DG,t*loss=∑i=1N(Pm,i,t*DG +Pm,i,t*SOP −Pm,i,t*L )−Pm,t*loss−cosφmSm,re,max* (37)Cm,OP,t=Cm,OP,tSOP+Cm,OP,tOLTC+Cm,OP,tCB

In this context, Pm,t*loss and Pm,DG,t*loss denote the per unit values of active network losses and curtailed wind and solar resources, respectively, for distribution network m during period t. The coefficients μloss and μDG represent the cost weights for network losses and renewable energy curtailment. Pm,DG,i,t* and Pm,load,i,t* denote the dispatched power from distributed generation and load demand at node i in distribution network m during period t. Costs COP,m,tSOP, COP,m,tOLTC, and COP,m,tCB correspond to the operational actions of the SOP, OLTC, and CB, respectively.

sec.title: 4.4. Model Transformation and Solution Process
sec.p: In the model mentioned above, the variables involve both SOP real and reactive power outputs as continuous variables, and actions of the OLTC and CB components as discrete variables. Essentially, it is a mixed-integer nonlinear programming problem, difficult to solve directly for optimization. This paper employs second-order cone relaxation to transform it into a mixed-integer second-order cone programming model, thus allowing the direct use of the CPLEX commercial solver for resolution. Nonlinear elements such as Im,ji,t2 and Um,i,t2 in Equations (41)–(46) are replaced by lm,ji,t and Vm,i,t. However, Equation (42) remains nonlinear, so it is relaxed into the following second-order cone constraints:(56)2Pm,ij,t2Qm,ij,tlm,ji,t−Vm,i,tT2<lm,ji,t+Vm,i,t
Constraints (27) containing quadratic nonlinearity can be transformed into the following rotated second-order cone constraints. (57) SiAC2≥Pi,tAC2+Qi,tAC2

sec.title: 5.1. Case Study Parameters
sec.p: This paper uses three improved IEEE 33 distribution networks to conduct a case study analysis on optimization strategies for multi-distribution network joint operation with the SOP under reverse power flow consideration. The topological structures of the three distribution networks are shown in Figure 11. The DG output and load forecast for each distribution network on a certain day are illustrated in Figure 12. It can be seen that in distribution network A, the DG output is high, maintaining reverse power flow throughout the day. In distribution network B, the DG output is moderate, with reverse power flow appearing during early morning and midday. In distribution network C, the DG output is low, with reverse power flow occurring only during the early morning.

The OLTC parameters in the three distribution networks are identical, with a rated transformation ratio KN of 110/11, a rated voltage UN of 110 kV, a rated capacity SN of 20 MVA, a rated power factor cosφT of 0.85, Pk of 112 kW, Uk% of 10.5%, high-voltage side taps of ±1.25% × 8, and a maximum number of actions within a scheduling cycle Km,ij,max=10.

In the reactive power compensation on the low-voltage side, the capacity of a single capacitor qm,CB,i=1MVA, with a total installation group number Nm,i,max=5, and a maximum number of operations per dispatch period ∆Nm,i,max=10.

In the utilized SOP, each VSC has a capacity of 5.0 MVA with a loss coefficient of 0.02. For the distribution networks A, B, and C, nodes connected to the SOP are selected according to the equivalent source method: A.5, B.14, and C.6 respectively. The model was tested on a PC with a 2.2 GHz main frequency and 32 GB of memory, using the MATLAB R2020b simulation platform. Embedded in this platform is the YALMIP mixed-integer optimization toolbox, which calls CPLEX version 12.8 for optimization solving [30].

sec.title: 5.2. Case Analysis
sec.p: To verify that the reverse power flow transmission capacity is insufficient in the DG high-penetration distribution networks, and by operating multiple distribution networks jointly through the SOP, the reverse power flow transmission capacity can be increased to reduce wind and solar curtailment, thus improving the operational efficiency of distribution networks. The following optimization scheme is established:
Scenario 1: Distribution networks A, B, and C operate independently.
Scenario 2: Distribution networks A and B operate jointly through a dual-port SOP.
Scenario 3: Distribution networks A, B, and C operate jointly through a tri-port SOP.

Scenario 1 serves as the original scheme. It examines the distribution network under varying operational characteristics such as the DG output, load demand, and topology. It analyzes the actions of the OLTC and CB, as well as wind and solar curtailment and network losses during independent operation. This serves as a reference for subsequent Scenarios (2 and 3) which involve the combined operation of two distribution networks. However, they differ in operational characteristics to explore optimization effects after interconnection. Scenario 4 involves three distribution networks operating jointly, allowing the exploration of how the number of interconnected distribution networks impacts optimization results. Specifically, it assesses whether more interconnected networks lead to improved optimization outcomes.

sec.title: 5.2.1. Analysis of Optimization Results During Independent Operation of Distribution Networks
sec.p: The scenario 1 analyzes the scenario where different distribution networks with varying operational characteristics rely solely on the OLTC and CB for optimization during independent operation. Figure 13, Figure 14 and Figure 15 show the results for distribution networks A, B, and C.

Comparing the operation of distribution networks A, B, and C, one can observe distinct DG placements. While network A’s DG lies closest to the OLTC and network B’s DG is further, all three networks show a similar active per unit value of maximal reverse power flow transfer capacity, approximately 0.37. Furthermore, permissible reverse power flow capacity varies directly with the tap changer ratio; a larger ratio increases capacity yet demands more reactive power compensation. Even at maximum tap ratio, reverse flow capacity remains below 50% of the OLTC’s rated capacity, significantly lower than the 80% target set in the design phase.

sec.title: 5.2.2. Optimized Results of the Joint Operation of Distribution Networks A and B
sec.p: In scenario 2, the situation of distribution network A and B after joint operation by SOP is analyzed. It can be seen in Figure 16 that the operation of distribution network A after joint operation has been improved compared with that after separate operation.

sec.title: 5.2.3. Optimization Results of the Joint Operation of Distribution Networks A, B, and C
sec.p: In Scenario 3, after the coordinated optimization of distribution networks A, B, and C through the SOP, the results improved significantly. As shown in Figure 17, the curtailment of wind and solar power in distribution network A improved.

sec.title: 6. Conclusions
sec.p:
This paper investigates the challenges posed by the increasing penetration of distributed generation (DG) in distribution networks, particularly concerning the management of reverse power flow. In Section 2, an analysis is conducted on three factors affecting reverse power flow in distribution networks: the parameters of the on-load tap changer (OLTC), the reactive power compensation capacity installed on both sides of the OLTC, and the electrical distance from the DG to the OLTC. The following conclusions are drawn:(1)
When transmitting reverse power flow, the OLTC, designed as a step-down transformer, is utilized as a step-up transformer. Consequently, even when the tap ratio of the OLTC reaches its limit, the ideal reverse power flow transmitted is only about 80% of its rated capacity. The specific impact of the OLTC tap ratio on the capacity for reverse power flow transmission is detailed in Equations (23) and (24) and Figure 6.(2)
The reactive power compensation capacity on both sides of the OLTC also influences the transmission of reverse power flow. Without additional reactive power compensation, insufficient reactive power capacity on the low-voltage side of the OLTC restricts the transmission of reverse power flow to approximately 30% of the rated capacity. However, by adding extra reactive power compensation on the low-voltage side, the capacity for reverse power flow transmission can be increased to about 80% of the OLTC’s rated capacity, albeit at the cost of additional installation, which raises the operational expenses of the distribution network.(3)
The electrical distance from the DG to the OLTC further limits the capacity for reverse power flow transmission, which can drop to around 30% of the OLTC’s capacity under the most adverse operating conditions.

Section 3 synthesizes the analysis of these three influencing factors and concludes that the impact of the OLTC tap ratio on reverse power flow transmission capacity is contradictory to the effect of the electrical distance from the DG to the OLTC. To address this, a parameter, bt is introduced to describe the voltage on the low-voltage side of the OLTC. This, combined with the aforementioned factors, leads to a precise method for calculating the capacity for reverse power flow transmission in distribution networks, as outlined in Table 1.

Section 4 establishes a joint operational optimization model for multiple distribution networks that includes an SOP to enhance the reverse power flow transmission capability of individual distribution networks. In the case studies presented in Section 5, the operational results of the distribution networks are analyzed under independent operation, dual network operation, and triple network operation, leading to the following conclusions:

When the distribution network operates independently, the capacity for reverse power flow is relatively poor, leading to significant curtailment of wind and solar energy when distributed generation (DG) output is high. However, interconnecting multiple distribution networks through the SOP can facilitate the sharing of reverse power flow capabilities among different networks, thereby reducing the curtailment of wind and solar energy and enhancing overall operational efficiency. Nonetheless, this approach requires further refinement, as joint operation largely depends on the operational conditions of the various distribution networks. If multiple distribution networks simultaneously need to export reverse power flow, the effectiveness of this method will be constrained. Additionally, the high costs associated with the SOP significantly limit the output capacity for reverse power flow.

Future research should consider the integration of energy storage systems (ESS) to form an E-SOP, which would allow for the storage of electricity during peak DG output periods and enable export during times when the joint system has surplus capacity for reverse power flow. This will be a focal point for the next phase of research.

The specific computational procedure for S2,re,t,max*.

tr.td: Input the data for the distribution network, including the internal impedance of the OLTC ZT*, the maximum transformation ratio Kmax*, the rated capacity SN*, the initial reactive power compensation on the low-voltage side, and the impedance from the equivalent DG node to the OLTC’s low-voltage side ZDG*.
Input the initial value of S2,re,t*, designating this initial value as the rated capacity of the OLTC, SN*. Set the transformation ratio for the OTLC as Kmax*.
Substitute the input data from Step 2 into Equation (7) to calculate the value of bt.

Evaluate whether bt falls within the permissible range. If it does not, revert to Step 1 and decrease the initial value of S2,re,t* accordingly until bt remains within the allowable limits. The current value of S2,re,t* represents the maximum transmission capacity S2,re,max* of the distribution network, considering only the OLTC transformation ratio.
Input the values of bt, Kmax*, and S2,re,t* into Equations (4) and (20) to calculate the magnitude of U3,t*.

Determine if U3,t* exceeds the limit. If it does, decrease S2,re,t* and return to Step 2. U3,t* is the highest voltage point in the distribution network. If U3,t* is within limits, other nodes will also be within limits.
Substitute the calculated S2,re,t* from Step 5 into Equation (19) to determine the required reactive compensation capacity QC2,re,t*.

To obtain S2,re,t* represents the maximum transmission capacity S2,re,max* of the distribution network under reverse flow, taking all factors into account, as well as the required reactive power compensation capacity, producing the output results.
